title: Major Holley takes up the bow and sings with his bass
summary: Few bassists took up the bow after him, but Major Holley, a friend since the late '30s, tried to outdo him, singing in his bass register.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Bass players: lineage, tone and technique

blocks.x: Yeah. Yeah, I remember that. That's quite a sound. That's -- you know, that's -- now when you -- did you begin to notice after you started using the bow that more bass players began using the bow in jazz during those years, or did the guys just continue to play mostly pizzicato?

Well, the fellows mostly continued to play, playing pizzicato. Maybe one or two bassists started using the bow after I had started, say like Major Holly. There's quite a story about old Major. We were the greatest of friends, of course, but Major told me during that time --

That was in the late '30s when we met. He told me that he was going to cut me every way but loose, you know. He was going to take my bow away from me and outdo me, that is, you know what I mean. And he's still trying to outdo me as of today.
And we are friends. You know what I mean? He does a fair job with it, you know. And --
Yeah, I have -- I like what he -- I like what he does, but it gets unmusical sometime to me.
I think it gets too much.

-- the thing of it is he tries. In fact, he sings in the same register as his bass, and it's rather harsh, I think, at times when you hear him right along, singing the same lyrics and in the same register as his bass, which is real low. And, of course, mine might sound a little different. My voice is one octave higher, you know, than my bass.

You know, I heard him do -- there was one period I heard him do something where he was singing a sixth away for a little while. But I don't think he's done any lately. I, you know, talked to him. I said, if he stays on this, then I'll have to deal with that. I think that just was -- maybe somebody needs to write him a letter and tell him to go back to sixths --
-- because that would be -- that's an interesting sound. It takes, you know, you really have to be thinking then.
